clue.text: Stream where jumping in is frowned upon (5)

definitions.text: Stream where jumping in is frowned upon

blocks.note: reads as a brook or river; here it is a steady line of people filing forward
not diving into water, but pushing in ahead of your turn

annotation.surface: A notice at a river or pool warning swimmers not to dive in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stream' and 'jumping in' conjure water and swimming; the stream is of people, and the jumping in is queue-jumping.
annotation.definitionFit: A queue is a line of people moving steadily forward, and cutting in is the classic breach of manners.

clue.text: Fifty under interrogation over vice uncovered in South Africa - curious! (9)

indicators.note: In a down entry, a piece 'under' the others is written below them, so L goes last.
In a down entry, 'over' puts QUIZ above what follows.
Uncovering a word strips off its outer letters.
The stripped vice sits inside ZA.

blocks.note: to quiz is to question closely
ZA is South Africa's international vehicle code
L is the Roman numeral for 50

annotation.surface: An interrogator digging into vice in South Africa, with a curious number fifty thrown in.
annotation.walkthrough: Because this is a down clue, 'under' and 'over' are positions on the page, not words about interrogation or crime.
annotation.definitionFit: Quizzical means puzzled or questioning, which is one sense of curious.

clue.text: Acclaim expressed from Sussex to Lancashire (5)

indicators.note: To express is to squeeze out, so the answer is pressed out of the words that follow.

annotation.surface: Praise voiced across England, from the south coast up to the north-west.
annotation.walkthrough: Sussex and Lancashire are English counties at opposite ends of the country; the answer straddles their names and the little word between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean to praise loudly and publicly.

clue.text: Schools with education provided by twice unfrocked priests (7)

indicators.note: Unfrocking strips the outer layer; doing it twice removes two letters from each end.

blocks.note: ed. is the standard short form of education
PRIESTS loses its outer letters twice: RIEST, then IES

annotation.surface: Schools run by priests who have been defrocked, and not just once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Schools' looks like a noun about institutions; it is a verb, to instruct. Unfrocking applied twice peels two layers off the priests.
annotation.definitionFit: To edify is to instruct and improve someone, as to school them does.

clue.text: Turntable parts used as visual aid? (4,5)

blocks.note: the record-deck word, split by 'parts' into TURN and TABLE
to flip is to turn over
a table of figures is a chart

annotation.surface: Bits of a record deck repurposed as a teaching prop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turntable' reads as a record player, but 'parts' tells you to split it into TURN and TABLE and replace each half.
annotation.definitionFit: A flip chart is a large pad of paper sheets on a stand, used to illustrate a talk.

clue.text: Loudly release time for church parade (6)

indicators.note: 'Time for church' asks for T to stand in place of CH.

annotation.surface: A noisy send-off timed for the church procession.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Church parade' sits together as a phrase, but 'church' belongs to the wordplay and 'parade' is the verb being defined.
annotation.definitionFit: To flaunt something is to parade it, showing it off conspicuously.

clue.text: Mainly undisclosed risks that could impact those cruising (8)

definitions.text: Mainly undisclosed risks that could impact those cruising

blocks.note: sounds like hidden small print; here it is mostly out of sight below the sea, the main

blocks.clueFragment: risks that could impact those cruising
blocks.note: reads as travel-insurance hazards; literally things a cruise ship could strike

annotation.surface: Small print in a holiday policy about hidden hazards for cruise passengers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mainly undisclosed' sounds like concealed terms and conditions; it is the bulk of an iceberg lying under the sea, with 'mainly' hinting at the main.
annotation.definitionFit: Icebergs are mostly submerged and a real collision danger to cruise ships.

clue.text: Screws, ones used by carpenters? (7)

blocks.note: to chisel someone is to cheat them, as to screw them is

annotation.surface: A question about which fixings a carpenter uses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screws' looks like a noun for fixings beside carpenters; it is the verb, to cheat.
annotation.definitionFit: Chisels are both cheats (verb) and the bladed tools carpenters cut wood with.

clue.text: Wholly effusive about fellows helping (9)

indicators.note: OTT goes about, around, the men.

annotation.surface: Someone gushing about the men who have lent a hand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like assistance; it is a noun, a portion allotted, as in a helping of pudding.
annotation.definitionFit: An allotment is a share handed out, just as a helping is a portion served.

clue.text: Control centre to work originally over start and end of Easter (5)

indicators.note: Originally means taking the first letter.
In a down entry 'over' puts the earlier pieces above the next.
Takes just the first and last letters.

blocks.note: E and R, the outside letters of Easter

annotation.surface: Mission control getting to work at the beginning and end of the Easter holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Control centre' is the airport control tower; 'to' is taken literally rather than as a link word.
annotation.definitionFit: A control tower is the centre from which air traffic is directed.

clue.text: One price, no frills, to enter new gallery complex (9)

indicators.note: Frills are the trimming at the edges, so removing them drops first and last letters.
The trimmed price goes inside TATE.

blocks.note: the Tate, the London art gallery

annotation.surface: A single budget ticket for a new gallery complex.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complex' reads as a noun for a group of buildings; it is the adjective, meaning complicated.
annotation.definitionFit: Intricate means detailed and complicated, which is what complex means.

clue.text: Favoured by a boring Liberal Welsh relative (2-3)

indicators.note: A drill boring into something ends up inside it, so A goes into L and W.

annotation.surface: A dull Welsh relation who happens to be the family favourite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' reads as dull, a fair insult for a relative; here it means drilling into.
annotation.definitionFit: A relation by marriage rather than blood, the classic being a mother-in-law.

clue.text: Huge amount of evil pervading religious community (7)

indicators.note: Something pervading spreads through the middle of what holds it.

blocks.note: Zion, the holy city and by extension the Jewish people

annotation.surface: A great deal of wickedness spreading through a religious group.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Huge amount of evil' looks like one phrase, but 'of' is the link and evil is only a piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A zillion is an informal word for an enormous, uncountable number.

clue.text: Dissident former pupil ousted by European sort of bouncer? (7)

indicators.note: OB is pushed out and E takes its place.

blocks.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil
E = European, slotted in where OB stood

annotation.surface: A rebellious ex-pupil thrown out by a European doorman.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that an ejector is only a sort of bouncer: someone or something that throws out, like a club bouncer.
annotation.definitionFit: A bouncer ejects people, so an ejector is a kind of bouncer.

clue.text: Out of the trap comes 26's rider? (6)

indicators.note: Trap is slang for mouth, so what comes out of it is spoken.

blocks.note: 26 across is TALON, and talons are claws

annotation.surface: A greyhound bursting from the trap with its jockey.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trap' suggests a starting gate at a dog track; it is British slang for the mouth, as in 'shut your trap'. A rider is an extra clause added to a document.
annotation.definitionFit: A rider is an additional clause attached to a contract or bill.

clue.text: An international such as Fitzgerald embraces power performance style (1,8)

indicators.note: The words around P hold it between them.

blocks.note: a cap is a player selected for their country, and so an international

annotation.surface: A national team player, like F. Scott Fitzgerald, packing a punch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Such as Fitzgerald' tempts toward the novelist F. Scott; it is the jazz singer, fitting because a cappella means singing without accompaniment.
annotation.definitionFit: A cappella is a style of singing performed without instruments.

clue.text: Paint finish for instance embeds good protective covering (8)

indicators.note: EG embeds G, setting it in its middle.

blocks.note: a shell protects what it covers

annotation.walkthrough: The whole surface is decorating advice, which hides that 'for instance' is simply EG.
annotation.definitionFit: Eggshell is a paint finish with a low sheen, between matt and silk.

clue.text: Security device in digital ledger rejecting intoduction of Bitcoins (4-5)

indicators.note: Drops the first letter of Bitcoins, B, from the ledger's name.

blocks.note: blockchain, the shared ledger behind cryptocurrencies
its first letter, removed from BLOCKCHAIN

annotation.walkthrough: The surface stays in the world of cryptocurrency, so 'security device' reads as software; it is a physical chain with a lock.

clue.text: 10's political self-determination (4,4)

blocks.note: the IN half of IN-LAW: to be in is to be at home
the LAW half of IN-LAW: a law is a rule

annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is not to an in-law as a person: each half of IN-LAW is swapped for a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Home rule is self-government for a region within a larger state.

clue.text: Get ahead of crazy golfer, nailing a putt at first (8)

indicators.note: Crazy tells you to scramble the letters.
To nail something is to fix it in place, so golfer holds A and P in its mix.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Crazy golf' pulls together in the surface, the mini-golf game, but 'crazy' is working alone on golfer.
annotation.definitionFit: From the playground game of vaulting over a crouching back, the verb means to overtake by jumping past.

clue.text: Gathered strip's an emphatic flop (7)

blocks.note: a gathered strip of fabric sewn on a skirt

annotation.surface: A dress trimming that proved a complete failure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flop' reads as failure; it means dropping down heavily, the kind of huffy movement a flounce is.
annotation.definitionFit: Flounce is both a frill of gathered fabric and an exaggerated, impatient movement.

clue.text: Church officer's given to unrestrained rich language (6)

indicators.note: Without its restraints at either end, rich loses first and last letters.

annotation.surface: A church official prone to florid, uninhibited speech.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rich language' pairs naturally as fruity swearing; 'rich' is wordplay and 'language' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Celtic is a family of languages, including Welsh and Irish; as a noun it names the language group.

clue.text: Loop back going through tortuous fens and swamps (7)

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all landscape, so 'swamps' reads as a noun; it is the verb, to overwhelm.

clue.text: Clean old style shaggy dog stories have this (6)

blocks.note: OS = Old Style, the pre-1752 calendar dating

annotation.definitionFit: Bathos is a sudden letdown from the lofty to the trivial, the payoff of a shaggy dog story.

clue.text: Upbraid a retrogressive tramp (7)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a noun for a vagrant; it is the verb, to roam. The little word 'a' carries PER.

annotation.definitionFit: Rates are prices, charges per unit.
